opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it started with languages before it had anything to do with computers. As a kid I was obsessed with how languages work: why Hindi and Urdu feel like one language when you speak them but look completely different on paper, why some words in Punjabi sound like cousins of English words. I'd go down rabbit holes reading about historical linguistics and sound changes, and I just loved that there was hidden structure in something everyone uses without thinking.

The computational side came in when I realized you could actually test those intuitions. Instead of arguing about how a language works, you could build a model, run it on data, and see what happens. That felt incredibly powerful. And then, of course, the field changed dramatically while I was getting into it. Language models went from these fairly brittle systems to things that seem to genuinely pick up a lot of linguistic structure on their own.

That raised the question that really hooked me: what have these models actually learned? Do they represent syntax the way linguists think about it, or something totally different? So computational linguistics became this nice intersection where I could keep the curiosity about human language I had as a kid and also work on what I think is one of the most important scientific questions right now, which is understanding what's going on inside these systems. It never felt like I had to choose between the linguistics and the AI. Each one makes the other more interesting.

r001.rationale: He connects computational linguistics to his childhood curiosity about language, but does not describe it as socially useful work.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it started with a pretty personal fascination with language itself. I grew up around multiple languages, and I was always struck by how much structure is hiding in something we use so effortlessly every day. You can have a five-year-old who's never heard the word "grammar" produce sentences that are perfectly well-formed, and nobody really taught them the rules explicitly. That gap between how easy language feels and how hard it is to describe formally just hooked me.

Then when I got into programming, I realized computational linguistics was the place where those two interests actually collided. You get to take these deep questions from linguistics, things like how meaning gets composed, how different languages encode the same ideas in completely different ways, and you get to make them concrete. You have to write it down precisely enough that a machine can do something with it. And the machine is a very honest critic. If your theory of how something works is wrong, it just fails, and that's incredibly clarifying.

The other thing that appealed to me was that it's a field where the data is everywhere. Humans have produced an unbelievable amount of text, in thousands of languages, and most of those languages have gotten almost no attention computationally. I found that really motivating, both as an intellectual puzzle and as a kind of unfinished project. There's so much linguistic diversity that the tools just didn't handle, and I wanted to be part of changing that.

And then, of course, the timing. I got into this right as neural models were starting to get genuinely good at language, and the questions shifted in a fascinating way. It went from "how do we get a machine to handle language at all" to "okay, this thing works, but what is it actually doing inside?" That interpretability question, trying to understand what these models have learned about language and whether it lines up with what linguists have believed for decades, felt like the most exciting open problem I could imagine working on. It's linguistics with a new kind of subject to study.

r001.rationale: Arora says computational linguistics brought together his personal fascination with language and programming, and that he wanted to improve computational tools for languages that had received little attention.

astra-6.text: What appealed to me was the combination of language and computation. Language is something we use so naturally, but when you try to describe how it works precisely enough for a computer to handle it, you realize how much complexity is hidden there. The same words can mean very different things depending on context. I liked that computational linguistics gave me a way to explore those questions concretely—to build something, test an idea, and learn from where it breaks down.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes interest in language and computation, but does not connect that interest to socially useful work.

sol-6.1.text:
What appealed to me was the intersection of language and computation. Language is something we use so naturally, but when you try to describe how it works precisely enough for a computer to handle it, you realize how much complexity is hidden underneath. The same words can mean different things depending on context, and people navigate that almost effortlessly.

I liked that computational linguistics gave me a way to explore those questions concretely. You can start with an idea about how language works, build a model, and see where it succeeds or breaks down. That connection between understanding something deeply human and approaching it computationally was really compelling to me.

r001.rationale: The response describes an interest in language and its computational study, but does not say this would connect that interest to socially useful work.
